items.title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
items.summary: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon? Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”. Continue reading...

items.summary: Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets. The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed. items.title: Iran proposes plan to reopen Hormuz within seven days
items.summary: Iran proposes plan to reopen Hormuz within seven days Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel. "Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi said at the UN Friday. "The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. "I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared." Earlier media reports suggest the new plan calls for a seven-day cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon.

On 23 September, "all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world," Bessent told CNBC in an interview as the war launched by the US and Israel nears the seven-month mark. "If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he added. The move follows earlier US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry and Bessent's "economic D-Day" threat on Iran and pledge to choke off Tehran financially.

items.title: Yemen crisis reminds Saudi Arabia of imperative to navigate tough realities
items.summary: For years, Saudi Arabia's security posture rested on a quiet assumption: that Washington would show up when it mattered. The dramatic events in Sept. 2019 tested that assumption directly. Claimed by Yemen’s Ansarullah movement but blamed on Iran, drone and missile strikes on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities knocked out roughly half of Saudi production overnight—one of the most consequential attacks on Gulf Arab energy infrastructure in decades. The United States did not respond militarily. That non-response is now widely read as the moment the assumption broke. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also discussed the war in the Middle East and the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. "The Foreign Secretary reiterated the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups on UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community," a Foreign Office statement said. A statement on Araghchi’s Telegram account said he had used the meeting to call for a correction to "the destructive and irresponsible approaches of some European governments towards Iran and regional developments." He also said an "insistence on interfering in countries’ internal affairs and the instrumental use of human rights concepts is in no way acceptable."

items.summary: Oil prices fall after Trump hails 'very productive' US-Iran talks at UN Oil prices fell on Wednesday after President Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had met for "very good" talks at the United Nations. The international benchmark, Brent crude, and main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, dipped to $98.91 and $89.93 per barrel respectively in early Asian trade -- well below the symbolic $100 mark they have smashed repeatedly since the Middle Eat war broke out in February. The three-hour meeting was "very good", "very productive" and "they have another one scheduled in the very near future", Trump told reporters as he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Trump's announcement came just hours after he delivered a bellicose address to the UN in which he said he faced a "big decision" on whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly". Report by AFP

items.summary: US refuses visas for Iran UN delegation members The United States has refused to issue visas to members of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's delegation, including his communications team, for this week's trip to the UN General Assembly, Iranian state media reported Monday. Pezeshkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to enter the US since the war began, with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. "In an unprecedented hostile move by the US government, (US President Donald) Trump has denied US visas to certain members of the president's high-level delegation, including members of his communications team," state news agency IRNA reported. The Mehr news agency also carried the story, citing a spokesperson for the Iranian presidency, and added that Pezeshkian would address the UN General Assembly on Wednesday.

items.title: Iran says it conveyed conditions to re-engage in talks, end war with US
items.summary: Iran says it conveyed conditions to re-engage in talks, end war with US Iran has conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in negotiations aimed at ending the war with the US, Iran's Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei said on Saturday in an interview with Al Jazeera. The conditions, which include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian funds and ending the naval blockade, had been communicated to the US via mediator Qatar, Rezaei stated, adding that a response from President Trump is awaited. Iran has become convinced of the need to change its strategy toward Washington following the US withdrawal from the memorandum of understanding, Rezaei stated. He said Iran knows the US military’s vulnerabilities and is more prepared than ever to counter its air strikes, adding that it recently tested an anti-ship missile near a US aircraft carrier. The security chief also said Iran seeks an end to the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. He believes the Houthis, too, seek an agreement with Saudi Arabia.

He said France had initiated an international defence mission with the International Maritime Organization last April aimed at escorting tankers and container ships through the strategic waterway once an agreement was reached. Macron said reopening Hormuz depended on a deal between Iran and the United States, which he said appeared unlikely in the short term. items.title: Colombia's new US-backed government cuts ties with Iran
items.summary: Colombia's new US-backed government cuts ties with Iran Colombia said on Thursday it had cut diplomatic ties with Iran, the latest Washington ally in Latin America to sever links with the US arch-foe. Colombia's new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has redrawn Colombia's alliances since taking over from his leftist predecessor Gustavo Petro on 7 August with the full-throated endorsement of US President Donald Trump. De la Espriella's government accused the Iranian government of having ties to "narco-terrorist groups that threaten the security of the country," without giving proof of the allegations. Iran's foreign ministry hit back on Friday, calling the allegations "baseless claims". "It is clear that none of the claims put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this decision has been made solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States."

items.title: Colombia formally cuts ties with Iran
items.summary: Colombia formally cuts ties with Iran Colombia on Thursday announced that it formally severed diplomatic relations with Iran, citing it "deteriorated" in Tehran. The Foreign Ministry said the decision took effect on Saturday due to "national and hemispheric security concerns," accusing Iran of human rights violations as well as alleged links to international terrorist and narcoterrorist groups. "Colombia also took into account confirmed human rights violations, verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities' obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran's nuclear program," the ministry said. "These facts deteriorated Colombia’s trust in the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran."

The mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which has been hemmed in by a lightning Houthi advance this month linked to the war on Iran. The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, and its southern and western rural areas, Reuters reported. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating from Houthi-controlled areas. The Iran-aligned Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces as they seek to consolidate gains made nearly two weeks ago, when their offensive along Yemen's western coast brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, through which at least ten percent of global maritime trade usually passes.

Despite persistent pressure from both Trump administration officials and President Donald Trump himself , most U.S. allies have remained reluctant . Those who have chosen to provide support have done so largely in an indirect capacity, such as by permitting limited base access. South Korea has been a major target of that pressure. items.title: Pakistan ready to implement Mecca pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, defence minister says
items.summary: Pakistan ready to implement Mecca pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, defence minister says Pakistan has said it is ready to implement its defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, amid recent Houthi attacks. Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said in an interview with Pakistani TV channel Geo News that the Mecca agreement - a defence deal between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey - "applies to us and we will fulfil our duty". He affirmed that Islamabad remains committed to protecting Saudi Arabia and its holy sites. Asif added that there was "absolutely no ambiguity" about the implementation of the defence pact, but did not disclose any further details about its defence strategy. He further said that Pakistan had conveyed Saudi Arabia's message to Iran over the Houthi attacks, and insisted that Iran would not "open another front".

items.summary: UN rights experts say US likely committed war crimes in Iran UN Human rights experts have confirmed following a fact-finding mission that they have "reasonable grounds" to believe that the US attacks on an Iranian school and a sports facility in February are tantamount to war crimes. One of the attacks included a 'double-tap' strike on an elementary school in the southern city of Minab on 28 February, killing 165 people, mostly students aged seven to 12. MEE reported at the time that a second strike killed sheltering survivors. The attack on sportshall in the nearby city of Lamerd killed at least 21 people, including dozens of teenage girls. A New York Times investigation found that the strike involved a newly developed US-made ballistic missile which had been untested in combat. items.title: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
items.summary: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until the United States meets “all of Iran’s conditions are met.” Under Iran's proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon; the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Thursday.

"We are facing a price crisis linking to a supply crisis," EU energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said in a letter to EU countries' energy ministers. While the EU is better prepared now than it was in winter 2021 when Russia squeezed Europe's gas supplies by reducing deliveries, governments must step up preparations for this winter, he said. "I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can sustain [gas storage] injections or reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary," Jorgensen said.

Hours earlier, Iraq’s state news agency had also reported the suspension of Iranian flights at Najaf International Airport over threats of US sanctions. The move means flights to and from Iran have been suspended at all four Iraqi airports where Iranian airlines were operating – Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniya – two sources told Reuters. items.summary: AI 'kill chain' contributed to Minab school killings: Bloomberg An Artificial Intelligence "kill chain" was behind the US missile strikes that killed more than 150 people - most of them children - at a school in Minab, southern Iran. According to a Bloomberg investigation , the Pentagon knows its overreliance on AI, which is fed with outdated targeting data and lacks human oversight, was behind the deadly strikes, which killed at least 123 children. Yashar Soltani, an Iranian investigative journalist, alleged that the Ministry of Petroleum has lost control of marketing and exporting the country's national oil industry, handing it to an exclusive network of four brokers who circumvent international sanctions. According to Soltani, Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former economic deputy at the intelligence organisation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, is overseeing the sale of Iranian oil and has, over the past three months, granted four brokers rights to sell 80m barrels of oil. The Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, Iraq's main export route other than the Strait of Hormuz, runs through Turkiye. Few have profited from this privatization of the U.S. military more than the CEOs of Pentagon contractors. While these companies often advertise their work as supporting the troops, the fact is that many servicemembers live in appalling housing conditions, while military-industrial contractors’ profits soar and their CEOs live in luxury. The lavish lifestyles of these CEOs is laid bare in the new mockumentary “Lords of War,” co-produced by the Quincy Institute and The Intercept. items.title: The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever | Editorial
items.summary: As the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challenges The United Nations was created, its charter states , to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran , another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles. The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking as he is in Washington to meet the US president. items.title: More money for Iran war? This rigmarole won't wash
items.summary: The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission. You shouldn’t go to war without the backing of the U.S. Congress. President Donald Trump is learning that the hard way, as his — not our — six-month-and-counting “ little excursion ” and “ small potatoes ” Iranian quagmire drags on. And you don’t build weapons for tomorrow’s wars — especially the ones you say are critical to future victories (remember them?) — using the parliamentary peek-a-boo prestidigitation known as reconciliation . In both instances, Trump is seeking big changes in U.S. national security as unilaterally as possible, with minimal congressional backing. Reconciliation is a controversial process to fund programs. It doesn’t have to follow the standard congressional appropriation rules. Most critically, reconciliation bills aren’t subject to a Senate filibuster . items.title: Hoe de Houthi's profiteren van het machtsvacuüm in Jemen
items.summary: Aan de opmars van de Houthi's in Jemen lijkt voorlopig geen einde te komen. Volgens persbureau Reuters proberen de door Iran gesteunde strijders nu ook het strategisch gelegen Kahboub-gebergte in het zuidwesten van Jemen in handen te krijgen. Als dat lukt, wordt de greep van de Houthi's op de Straat van Bab al-Mandab nog steviger. En dat terwijl de Houthi's een maand geleden alleen nog het noordwesten van Jemen onder controle hadden. Sinds juli is het geweld tussen de militante groepering en Saudi-Arabië opgelaaid, en onlangs begonnen de Houthi's een grondoffensief. Daarbij namen ze al de steden Mokka en Dhubab en het eiland Perim in, waarmee het de controle over de belangrijke zeestraat Bab al-Mandab in handen kreeg. Die is belangrijk voor de internationale zeevaart, zeker nu de Straat van Hormuz sinds februari vrijwel afgesloten is vanwege de oorlog tussen de VS en Iran. Daarmee hebben de Houthi's een belangrijke troef in handen. Toch ondervonden ze weinig weerstand bij hun opmars naar de zeestraat. Hoe konden de Houthi's zo snel en ogenschijnlijk makkelijk oprukken? items.summary: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy We’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in a matter of weeks . Prices are rising, troop morale is plummeting , and there is little evidence things will improve. The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recently threatened to “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doing idiotic stunts on YouTube and getting hit in the face during boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department of War Crimes ?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech. In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzinger wrote , “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.”

items.title: Trump still thinks Iranians will ‘rise up’ against the government. In Tehran I see a different story | Hossein Hamdieh
items.summary: If anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this point The US president, Donald Trump, asked recently on one of his Truth Social rants : “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” So frenetic and all-over-the-place are Trump’s statements that one does not know which are actual policies and which are simply noise. But if counting on the “Iranian people” to rise up and fight is indeed US policy then, as far as I can tell from within Iran, it is a failed one. And miserably so. At least for now. There is no reliable nationwide polling that can tell us what Iranians think about the war in real time. So this is an observation, not a poll. It comes from conversations I have had with many people. Hossein Hamdieh holds a joint PhD in Geography and Anthropology from Humboldt University of Berlin and King’s College London. The panic started shortly after the ex-Anthropic, ex-OpenAI researcher-turned-whistleblower, Jacob Coxon sounded the alarm on X , writing that AI companies are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s diagnosis is startling. AI, he wrote, “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” In a shocking turn, Anthropic’s own Evan Hubinger confirmed growing fears when he wrote, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade." It’s no surprise that dire remarks like this from AI experts have turned every news headline or cable news segment this week into a freak-out over the coming doomsday . But is all of this panic really warranted? In the latest episode of Always at War , we attempt to parse what’s actually dangerous about AI from cynical industry hype. clusters.headline: China is outfoxing the US in the battle for Mideast influence

items.title: China is outfoxing the US in the battle for Mideast influence
items.summary: Washington talks about “influence” as though it were a mystical vapor that leaks out of every military base closure. But Beijing’s rapidly growing clout in the Middle East shows that influence can come in many forms. While the Pentagon debates whether and where to rebuild U.S. bases battered by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, China has spent the last decade expanding its influence in the Middle East without stationing a single soldier there. China’s experience in the region makes clear that influence can be cultivated far more cheaply than Washington assumes, and without maintaining a sprawling network of vulnerable military installations. As Operation Epic Fury demonstrated, Washington’s constellation of fixed bases across the Middle East is vulnerable and expensive to defend. Before the war, the United States maintained at least 19 military facilities across the region, eight of them considered permanent. clusters.headline: When Saudi Arabia realizes it's backed the wrong horse

items.title: When Saudi Arabia realizes it's backed the wrong horse
items.summary: The United States went to war with Iran in the belief that American power could quickly overwhelm Tehran’s ability to threaten the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, the war is producing nearly the opposite result. Iran has been badly hit, but it and its regional allies have demonstrated that they can still threaten Saudi cities, oil installations, pipelines and export routes. At the same time, Washington has shown that even overwhelming offensive power does not necessarily translate into effective protection for its Gulf partners. The consequence is likely to be a historic Saudi reassessment: less confidence in the United States, more reliance on regional partners and a much closer strategic relationship with China. Saudi Arabia’s geographical problem is not new. In an article published in LobeLog in September 2019 , I described the “encirclement” of Saudi oil production by Iran and Iran-aligned forces. items.title: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support
items.summary: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a limited time, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region. Riyadh requested support after the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. "We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling," he told reporters as he travelled to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. "Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack... and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request," he said.

items.summary: With the US midterm elections now just six weeks away, we’ll speak to our Washington correspondent Fraser Jackson about whether President Donald Trump could help or hurt his party’s chances. Polls have pointed to what some are calling a “blue wave”, with Democrats potentially regaining control of the House, while the Senate race remains more uncertain. Trump has ramped up campaigning, including spending heavily on advertising and proposing $5,000 payments to voters who support Republicans. But with his approval ratings under pressure amid the war in Iran and the Middle East, and rising oil, gasoline and commodity prices compared with before he took office, the political landscape could still shift significantly in the coming weeks.

Explosions at a weapons depot in the early hours of Monday in al-Eis, southern Aleppo, wounded at least four. items.summary: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday said that Tehran must fight and negotiate as its near seven-month war with the United States drags on. Addressing the parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran would use its military might to “push the enemy back and deal them devastating blows” at crucial junctures, but would resort to diplomacy when it has the upper hand on the battlefield. The Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States fulfilled its commitments, according to Ghalibaf, who said Iran's negotiating position was “entirely clear, rational, and non-negotiable”. His remarks come after Pakistani and Qatari mediators have reportedly been told that Iran has seven conditions which must be met before talks with Washington can begin.

items.summary: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States fulfils its commitments under a June agreement and meets Tehran’s conditions. Speaking in parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran had “explicitly conveyed its conditions to the opposing side through intermediaries”, according to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB. Reuters has previously reported that Tehran has tied the reopening of the strait to US commitments under the June memorandum, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, oil sanctions and other measures. “The enemy is well aware that the path of deception and unilateral imposition is closed,” Ghalibaf said, adding that there would be no return to negotiations or reopening of the waterway until Iran’s rights were recognised and US commitments fulfilled. The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for global oil and gas shipments, and traffic through the waterway has remained sharply below pre-war levels amid the continuing tensions.

Baghaei said that the country had a duty to attend the most important international event to make the rights of the Iranian people heard by the world. items.summary: Iran disputes US oil claim, approves new rule on Hormuz data cables Iran has disputed a claim by US Central Command (Centcom) that it escorted tankers carrying more than a billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi called the claim a “failed psychological operation” meant to boost US troop morale and justify the war’s financial and human costs, Iran’s Fars news agency reported. Centcom had also said it protected more than 2,000 commercial transits through the strait and cleared its main shipping lanes of mines, in addition to facilitating oil exports. Separately, a committee of senior Iranian officials has approved a rule requiring Tehran’s approval for data cables routed through the strait, Fars reported. The measure, known as Article 10, will also apply to other data communications equipment passing through the waterway, with further details to be set out in upcoming regulations.

items.title: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence
items.summary: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday called for greater reliance on dialogue, cooperation and multilateral institutions. Speaking virtually at Indonesia's Global Town Hall 2026, Araghchi said: "Sustainable security in the Middle East cannot be dictated from outside the region." Araghchi said ignoring international law when it conflicts with the interests of major powers undermines the rule of law, while the failure of international institutions such as the United Nations to respond to aggression and hold violators accountable could damage their credibility. "We believe that sustainable security can be achieved through dialogue, trust-building, cooperation and mutual respect among the countries of the region, not through the military presence of foreign powers and the imposition of their will," he said.

items.title: Prix du carburant: «Les véritables tensions sont sur le marché du raffinage»
items.summary: La flambée du prix des carburants relance la colère sociale. De nombreuses manifestations ont eu lieu un peu partout dans le monde ces derniers jours, face aux pénuries et à la hausse du coût de la vie. En Syrie, en France, aux États-Unis ou au Guatemala, où les chauffeurs de taxi et les travailleurs des transports se sont mobilisés en bloquant quatre points de la capitale et certains axes de l'intérieur du pays. Après le blocage iranien du détroit d'Ormuz, par où transite habituellement 20 % du commerce mondial d'hydrocarbures, un nouveau front s'est ouvert la semaine passée dans le détroit de Bab-el-Mandeb, après que les houthistes pro-iraniens en ont pris le contrôle. items.summary: Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestinian delegation from upcoming UN General Assembly On Thursday, 152 countries voted in favour of a resolution adopted by the UN General Assembly, rejecting the US's decision to prevent the Palestinian delegation from participating in the upcoming UN General Assembly session in New York City. The resolution called on Washington to reverse the decision, considering it a clear violation of the Headquarters Agreement, which legally obliges the host country to facilitate the entry of diplomatic delegations. The US State Department said on Thursday it has greenlit visas for a core Iranian delegation and essential staffers to take part in the meeting, but denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and other Palestinian officials visas.

items.title: «Les deux vies et trois morts» du réalisateur iranien Karim Lakzadeh
items.summary: C'est une fable acerbe de l’Iran aujourd’hui, macabre et burlesque, avec un équilibre parfait entre l’humour noir et une critique sociale féroce. Dans le film Living Twice, Dying Thrice (« Deux vies, trois morts »), Karim Lakzadeh, né en 1986 à Chiraz, dans la province du Fars en Iran, raconte l’histoire de trois mineurs qui traversent le pays clandestinement. Victimes de l’effondrement d’une mine, ils décident de se faire déclarer morts pour commencer une deuxième vie. Présenté en première mondiale au Festival de Cannes, le film sera projeté au cinéma Louxor, à Paris, à l’occasion de la reprise de la programmation de l’ACID, du 17 au 20 septembre, dédiée au renouvellement des regards cinématographiques.

items.summary: For a decade, Saudi Arabia’s Yemen policy has rested on the assumption that time, money and coercive force, patiently and strategically applied, would eventually produce enough leverage to subdue the Houthis, or at least force them into a settlement on Riyadh’s terms. Over the last two weeks, that assumption has been tested more severely than at any point since 2015, when Saudi Arabia initially launched its military intervention to roll back Houthi control of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. It has not held. Having seized strategically significant swathes of Yemen’s west coast on the Red Sea, the Houthis are now pressing towards Marib, the last major stronghold of forces loyal to the internationally-recognized government of Yemen, and the site of some of the country’s most important oil and gas facilities. If losing the Red Sea coast was a blow to the government, losing Marib would be a decisive defeat. items.title: The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
items.summary: The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait. The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate , a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. Speaking ahead of a visit to France, Aoun said Lebanon had “no choice” but negotiations, warning that the alternative would be a costly war. items.title: The truth behind Donald Trump’s ‘biggest oil deal in world history’
items.summary: The US’s oil deal with Venezuela faces multiple legal and logistical problems, including questions about whether it can be implemented Donald Trump has long coveted the oilfields of other nations and declared an agreement with Venezuela to be “the biggest oil deal in world history”. But the deal, reached after the US seized Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, is almost certainly doomed to collapse amid a wide array of legal and logistical issues, a Guardian investigation has found. The US president first mused about taking oil from Iran in 1987, when he told ABC’s Barbara Walters that Iranian attacks on American shipping during the Iran-Iraq war required an extreme response. “Why couldn’t we go in and take over some of their oil, which is along the sea?” he asked. Over the ensuing years, he has returned frequently to the idea that America should seize oil from other countries after military conflict, from Libya to Iraq. Continue reading...

items.title: Iran proposes plan to reopen Hormuz within seven days
items.summary: Iran proposes plan to reopen Hormuz within seven days Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel. "Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi said at the UN Friday. "The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. "I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared." Earlier media reports suggest the new plan calls for a seven-day cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon.

items.summary: EU warns of energy 'price crisis', asks countries to consider curbing demand The European Union is facing an energy price crisis as a result of the Iran war fallout in oil and gas markets, the bloc's energy chief said on Friday in a letter seen by Reuters, which urged countries to consider measures to curb energy demand. "We are facing a price crisis linking to a supply crisis," EU energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said in a letter to EU countries' energy ministers. While the EU is better prepared now than it was in winter 2021 when Russia squeezed Europe's gas supplies by reducing deliveries, governments must step up preparations for this winter, he said. "I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can sustain [gas storage] injections or reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary," Jorgensen said.

items.summary: Turkish parliament speaker expects Pakistan, Saudi Arabia defence pact to be submitted for approval next month A joint defence pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan has not yet been submitted to the Turkey's parliament for approval, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus said on Friday, adding he expected the agreement to be formally submitted when parliament returns from recess next month. The regional powers signed the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement" in August, weeks before Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launched attacks against Saudi Arabia amid the war in Iran. Similar to NATO's Article 5, the pact stipulates that an attack on one ally constitutes an attack on all. "For international agreements to come into effect, parliamentary approval is needed. The meetings held as part of the agreement at the moment are preparatory meetings," Kurtulmus told reporters in Ankara.

Hours earlier, Iraq’s state news agency had also reported the suspension of Iranian flights at Najaf International Airport over threats of US sanctions. The move means flights to and from Iran have been suspended at all four Iraqi airports where Iranian airlines were operating – Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniya – two sources told Reuters. The US had announced it would impose sanctions on any global companies doing business with Iranian airlines after 23 September, with the aim of grounding Iran's entire civilian fleet worldwide.

items.title: UK warns Iran it will not tolerate hostile activity on its soil
items.summary: UK warns Iran it will not tolerate hostile activity on its soil Britain's foreign minister met his Iranian counterpart on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York and told him his country would "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil" from groups linked to Iran. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also discussed the war in the Middle East and the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. "The Foreign Secretary reiterated the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups on UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community," a Foreign Office statement said. A statement on Araghchi’s Telegram account said he had used the meeting to call for a correction to "the destructive and irresponsible approaches of some European governments towards Iran and regional developments." He also said an "insistence on interfering in countries’ internal affairs and the instrumental use of human rights concepts is in no way acceptable."

Some 250 miles away, U.S. missiles fell on a residential area of Lamerd, killing 21 civilians, including five children. Neither the White House nor Pentagon has publicly admitted responsibility in either incident, although an internal review reportedly determined Minab was hit by a U.S. missile. items.title: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces
items.summary: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces Yemen's Saudi-backed forces said on Thursday that they had repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to the southern port city of Aden, where the government is based. The mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which has been hemmed in by a lightning Houthi advance this month linked to the war on Iran. The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, and its southern and western rural areas, Reuters reported. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating from Houthi-controlled areas. The Iran-aligned Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces as they seek to consolidate gains made nearly two weeks ago, when their offensive along Yemen's western coast brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, through which at least ten percent of global maritime trade usually passes.

items.title: Yemen crisis reminds Saudi Arabia of imperative to navigate tough realities
items.summary: For years, Saudi Arabia's security posture rested on a quiet assumption: that Washington would show up when it mattered. The dramatic events in Sept. 2019 tested that assumption directly. Claimed by Yemen’s Ansarullah movement but blamed on Iran, drone and missile strikes on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities knocked out roughly half of Saudi production overnight—one of the most consequential attacks on Gulf Arab energy infrastructure in decades. The United States did not respond militarily. That non-response is now widely read as the moment the assumption broke. items.summary: The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission. You shouldn’t go to war without the backing of the U.S. Congress. President Donald Trump is learning that the hard way, as his — not our — six-month-and-counting “ little excursion ” and “ small potatoes ” Iranian quagmire drags on. And you don’t build weapons for tomorrow’s wars — especially the ones you say are critical to future victories (remember them?) — using the parliamentary peek-a-boo prestidigitation known as reconciliation . In both instances, Trump is seeking big changes in U.S. national security as unilaterally as possible, with minimal congressional backing. Reconciliation is a controversial process to fund programs. It doesn’t have to follow the standard congressional appropriation rules. Most critically, reconciliation bills aren’t subject to a Senate filibuster . items.summary: Report: Hormuz traffic on Tuesday below 10-day average Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday. The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage. All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT. One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data. The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Iran conflict. Meanwhile, 22 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, another maritime chokepoint on the southwest tip of Yemen and a vital trade route for oil between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. items.title: The Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencers | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy We’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in a matter of weeks . Prices are rising, troop morale is plummeting , and there is little evidence things will improve. The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recently threatened to “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doing idiotic stunts on YouTube and getting hit in the face during boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department of War Crimes ?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech. In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzinger wrote , “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.”

items.title: Trump still thinks Iranians will ‘rise up’ against the government. In Tehran I see a different story | Hossein Hamdieh
items.summary: If anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this point The US president, Donald Trump, asked recently on one of his Truth Social rants : “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” So frenetic and all-over-the-place are Trump’s statements that one does not know which are actual policies and which are simply noise. But if counting on the “Iranian people” to rise up and fight is indeed US policy then, as far as I can tell from within Iran, it is a failed one. And miserably so. At least for now. There is no reliable nationwide polling that can tell us what Iranians think about the war in real time. So this is an observation, not a poll. It comes from conversations I have had with many people. Hossein Hamdieh holds a joint PhD in Geography and Anthropology from Humboldt University of Berlin and King’s College London. items.title: China is outfoxing the US in the battle for Mideast influence
items.summary: Washington talks about “influence” as though it were a mystical vapor that leaks out of every military base closure. But Beijing’s rapidly growing clout in the Middle East shows that influence can come in many forms. While the Pentagon debates whether and where to rebuild U.S. bases battered by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, China has spent the last decade expanding its influence in the Middle East without stationing a single soldier there. China’s experience in the region makes clear that influence can be cultivated far more cheaply than Washington assumes, and without maintaining a sprawling network of vulnerable military installations. As Operation Epic Fury demonstrated, Washington’s constellation of fixed bases across the Middle East is vulnerable and expensive to defend. Before the war, the United States maintained at least 19 military facilities across the region, eight of them considered permanent. items.title: When Saudi Arabia realizes it's backed the wrong horse
items.summary: The United States went to war with Iran in the belief that American power could quickly overwhelm Tehran’s ability to threaten the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, the war is producing nearly the opposite result. Iran has been badly hit, but it and its regional allies have demonstrated that they can still threaten Saudi cities, oil installations, pipelines and export routes. At the same time, Washington has shown that even overwhelming offensive power does not necessarily translate into effective protection for its Gulf partners. The consequence is likely to be a historic Saudi reassessment: less confidence in the United States, more reliance on regional partners and a much closer strategic relationship with China. items.title: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support
items.summary: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a limited time, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region. Riyadh requested support after the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. "We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling," he told reporters as he travelled to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. "Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack... and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request," he said.

items.summary: With the US midterm elections now just six weeks away, we’ll speak to our Washington correspondent Fraser Jackson about whether President Donald Trump could help or hurt his party’s chances. Polls have pointed to what some are calling a “blue wave”, with Democrats potentially regaining control of the House, while the Senate race remains more uncertain. Trump has ramped up campaigning, including spending heavily on advertising and proposing $5,000 payments to voters who support Republicans. But with his approval ratings under pressure amid the war in Iran and the Middle East, and rising oil, gasoline and commodity prices compared with before he took office, the political landscape could still shift significantly in the coming weeks.

Conceived as a protector of the Iranian revolution, the guard has hundreds of thousands of troops who are distinct from Iran’s official army. It is also unelected, sitting alongside Iran’s elected officials under the ultimate authority of the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei . The IRGC was founded in March 1979 by commanders of the conservative militias that helped overthrow the western-backed Shah Reza Pahlavi the previous month. Trump also said he was open to the idea of meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week. He did, however, claim it was impossible for the US to reach a deal,  as some Iranian officials are "hiding like rats". The US president also confirmed that his administration remained in constant contact with the Houthis who, according to him, agreed not to fight the US military. items.title: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on
items.summary: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday said that Tehran must fight and negotiate as its near seven-month war with the United States drags on. Addressing the parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran would use its military might to “push the enemy back and deal them devastating blows” at crucial junctures, but would resort to diplomacy when it has the upper hand on the battlefield. The Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States fulfilled its commitments, according to Ghalibaf, who said Iran's negotiating position was “entirely clear, rational, and non-negotiable”. His remarks come after Pakistani and Qatari mediators have reportedly been told that Iran has seven conditions which must be met before talks with Washington can begin.

items.title: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States fulfils its commitments under a June agreement and meets Tehran’s conditions. Speaking in parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran had “explicitly conveyed its conditions to the opposing side through intermediaries”, according to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB. Reuters has previously reported that Tehran has tied the reopening of the strait to US commitments under the June memorandum, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, oil sanctions and other measures. “The enemy is well aware that the path of deception and unilateral imposition is closed,” Ghalibaf said, adding that there would be no return to negotiations or reopening of the waterway until Iran’s rights were recognised and US commitments fulfilled. The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for global oil and gas shipments, and traffic through the waterway has remained sharply below pre-war levels amid the continuing tensions.

items.title: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US
items.summary: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei has said that Iran will not abandon its right to be present in the UN General Assembly, stressing that attending the UN meeting is not a privilege given by Washington, according to IRNA. Speaking in a televised programme, Baghaei said that being in New York held absolutely no charm for Iranian representatives, but it was a "trench that must not be abandoned". He said participating in the UN General Assembly was a legal right rather than a favour from others, as Iran was one of the 50 founding member states of the UN. Baghaei said that the country had a duty to attend the most important international event to make the rights of the Iranian people heard by the world. He added that the US "used every tool to prevent the Iranian delegation’s participation, ranging from derogatory remarks and media propaganda to abusing its commitments as the host government by creating delays or refusing to issue visas for several delegation members", IRNA reported.

Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi called the claim a “failed psychological operation” meant to boost US troop morale and justify the war’s financial and human costs, Iran’s Fars news agency reported. Centcom had also said it protected more than 2,000 commercial transits through the strait and cleared its main shipping lanes of mines, in addition to facilitating oil exports. Separately, a committee of senior Iranian officials has approved a rule requiring Tehran’s approval for data cables routed through the strait, Fars reported. The measure, known as Article 10, will also apply to other data communications equipment passing through the waterway, with further details to be set out in upcoming regulations.

items.summary: Matthew Bunn on the factors driving the risk of nuclear war — and how we shift them toward greater safety, for ourselves and for future generations. Location: The Foundry, 101 Rogers St, Cambridge Some of the most consequential decisions our civilization makes — decisions that will shape the lives of countless future generations — concern nuclear weapons and the risk of nuclear war. Harvard's Matthew Bunn will join Long Now Boston to take the long view on one of humanity's defining challenges. A nuclear war is unlikely to come "out of a clear blue sky." It is far more likely to arise from a crisis or conflict between nuclear-armed states that escalates step by step. Bunn offers a structured way of thinking about reducing the risk at each of those steps: lowering the chance of conflict among nuclear-armed states in the first place; keeping any conflict that does occur from crossing the nuclear threshold; and ensuring that, if nuclear weapons are ever used, the exchange does not escalate to hundreds or thousands of weapons. The conditions, which include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian funds and ending the naval blockade, had been communicated to the US via mediator Qatar, Rezaei stated, adding that a response from President Trump is awaited. Iran has become convinced of the need to change its strategy toward Washington following the US withdrawal from the memorandum of understanding, Rezaei stated. He said Iran knows the US military’s vulnerabilities and is more prepared than ever to counter its air strikes, adding that it recently tested an anti-ship missile near a US aircraft carrier. The security chief also said Iran seeks an end to the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. He believes the Houthis, too, seek an agreement with Saudi Arabia.

items.title: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence
items.summary: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday called for greater reliance on dialogue, cooperation and multilateral institutions. Speaking virtually at Indonesia's Global Town Hall 2026, Araghchi said: "Sustainable security in the Middle East cannot be dictated from outside the region." Araghchi said ignoring international law when it conflicts with the interests of major powers undermines the rule of law, while the failure of international institutions such as the United Nations to respond to aggression and hold violators accountable could damage their credibility. "We believe that sustainable security can be achieved through dialogue, trust-building, cooperation and mutual respect among the countries of the region, not through the military presence of foreign powers and the imposition of their will," he said.

But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports.
